new_statements.rule_in_words: A vowel is stressed if it is long and word-final (case a); otherwise the vowel of the penultimate syllable is stressed (case b); the two cases are disjunctively ordered, so a final long vowel (e.g. from -shaq/-raq -> [a:] by 'length by coalescence', rule 5.1, which must precede stress placement) takes the stress ([aywashá:] beside [aywáshaq]), else the penult. Equivalent to the catalog's 'stress the penultimate mora'.
new_statements.exceptions: p.74: the author is 'not sure how this rule [3.3, optional deletion of the vowel of word-final -mi, -shi, -si, -shqa] interacts with rule (9) (stress placement)': noqa-si -> [noqás] ~ [nóqas] 'I also'; p.78: word-final imperative/infinitive -y after i does not attract stress to the final syllable and long/short vowels do not contrast in unstressed word-final syllables; length 'fore-shortening' suffixes (5.2) remove underlying length before certain suffixes.
new_statements.identity_note: Weber 1983/1989/1996 and Rimaycuna describe Huallaga (Huánuco) Quechua (qub) as spoken along the Huallaga river in Huánuco department; Weber 1976 draws its data from Llacón, Huánuco (principal consultant Teodoro Cayco, native of Maray, one day's walk from Llacón; 'a few differences.. do not concern us here', note 2 p.91), which SIL's archive files under Huallaga Huánuco Quechua [qub]; Teodoro Cayco is also a co-author of Rimaycuna. Toliver 1989 is catalogued by SIL under Ambo-Pasco Quechua [qva] although Glottolog lists it under hual1241.

new_statements.quote: (p.590) 23.6 El acento. El acento se asigna básicamente a la penúltima mora.[10] En el caso más común, la penúltima sílaba es acentuada; por ejemplo: /ayway/ [áyway] 've, anda (IMP)' /aywaykan/ [aywáykan] 'están yendo' /aywaykanmi/ [aywaykánmi] 'están yendo (DIR)' /aywašaykikama/ [aywašaykikáma] 'hasta que vayas'. Puesto que las vocales largas se cuentan como dos moras, las vocales largas en posición final de palabra llevan acento. ... /mana-raq/ [manáraq] ~ [manará:] 'todavía no' ... Puesto que la penúltima mora recibe el acento, y puesto que el sufijo de primera persona (verbal o no verbal) es la cantidad vocálica, es decir una mora, siempre lleva el acento salvo cuando aparece antes de la penúltima. [fn.10: La mora es la medida mínima de duración. Una vocal corta mide una mora; una vocal larga mide dos moras.]
new_statements.translation: 23.6 Stress. Stress is basically assigned to the penultimate mora. In the most common case the penultimate syllable is stressed, e.g. [áyway] 'go (IMP)', [aywáykan] 'they are going', [aywaykánmi] 'they are going (DIR)', [aywašaykikáma] 'until you go'. Since long vowels count as two moras, word-final long vowels carry the stress ... [manáraq] ~ [manará:] 'not yet' ... Since the penultimate mora receives the stress, and since the first-person suffix (verbal or non-verbal) is vowel length, i.e. one mora, it always carries the stress except when it stands before the penult. [fn.10: The mora is the minimal unit of duration; a short vowel measures one mora, a long vowel two.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the syllable containing the penultimate mora: normally the penult, but a word-final long vowel (two moras: underlying final length, first-person length suffix, or compensatory length from a dropped /q/) is stressed; the first-person length suffix is stressed unless it stands before the penult.

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, default penult, final stress only when the final vowel is long, CVV heavy / CVC light) matches Weber's explicit rule 'stress is assigned to the penultimate mora.. long vowels count as two mora, word-final long vowels are stressed', verified on the page scan of the held dissertation at the cited locator (23.7, p. 424 = PDF 457, fn. 378), with the CVC-light inference supported by his own example [aywáykaŋ]/[aywaykáŋmi] and corroborated by 23.8.5 (apocope shifts stress) and 23.9.1.3 (loans take native penult stress, [bálkoŋ]). The source is the language's reference grammar by its principal describer; the only 'better' items are later editions of the same work (1989 English, 1996 Spanish), which are unlikely to change the rule. No independent phonology/instrumental study of Huallaga stress was found in Glottolog's list; web search was unavailable

tone.quote: En el quechua del Huallaga, el acento recae en la penúltima sílaba; por tanto, es grave. Esta es una característica general de todas las variedades del quechua 11. Por ello, en el corpus que analizamos, evidenciamos que, en los casos de las palabras prestadas agudas y esdrújulas, se realiza un desplazamiento acentual hacia la penúltima sílaba; es decir que los hablantes adaptan el acento al patrón patrimonial del quechua. [...] Por tanto, en términos fonológicos, el quechua pertenece al tipo de acento fijo, a diferencia del español, donde el acento es parcialmente libre.
tone.locator: p. 39, section 2.3.3 'El acento en el español y quechua'; '11' is a footnote call (fn. 11: Julca 2009 records oxytone words for affective states, interjections and onomatopoeia)
tone.translation: In Huallaga Quechua, stress falls on the penultimate syllable; it is therefore paroxytone. This is a general characteristic of all varieties of Quechua [fn. 11]. Hence, in the corpus we analyse, we find that in borrowed oxytone and proparoxytone words the stress shifts to the penultimate syllable; that is, speakers adapt the stress to the native Quechua pattern. [...] Therefore, in phonological terms, Quechua belongs to the fixed-stress type, unlike Spanish, where stress is partially free.
